notes: \cpara{Sets the scene without naming an experiment. Gilbert, Krull and Malone's 1990 paper points to wider evidence: in research on attribution, persuasion and lie detection, ``instances of inappropriate belief'' are, ``in general,'' ``exacerbated by cognitive load and interruption.''}
\cpara{Introduces Gilbert's question: do we believe everything we are told?}

\cpara{States the two models as Gilbert and colleagues state them. For Spinoza, in their words, all ideas are ``accepted (i.e., represented in the mind as true) prior to a rational analysis of their veracity.''}

\cpara{The first sentence sits uneasily with the post's own source. Gilbert, Krull and Malone write that philosophers such as Reid and Russell ``found cause to question the Cartesian distinction,'' and that what ``continues to embrace'' it is ``modern psychology.''}
\cfact{The footnote cites a post by Robin Hanson about policy debates. It does not mention Descartes, Spinoza or philosophers, so the sentence it is attached to has no source.}
\cpara{States the two predictions as the 1990 paper does: interruption should make a Spinozan mind ``mistake false ideas for true ones, but not vice versa.''}

\cpara{Reports Study 1 correctly: 55\% and 58\% correct for true statements, 55\% and 35\% for false ones. The figures rest on 35 students, each of whom had two interrupted true statements and two interrupted false ones.}

\clogic{The results fit Spinoza's model, but the model was already disputed when the post appeared (see also the note on ``Your Strength as a Rationalist''). Hasson, Simmons and Todorov (\textsc{Psychological Science}, 2005) found the same asymmetry only for statements that tell you little when false, not for statements that are informative when false, and concluded that ``comprehending a statement may not require believing it.'' Later, Nadarevic and Erdfelder (\textsc{Memory \& Cognition}, 2013) reported results that they said ``clearly contradict the Spinozan model.''}

\cpara{Describes Experiment 1 of the 1993 paper accurately: statements in red were false, the busy group searched for the digit 5, and prison terms ran from 0 to 20 years. The subjects were 71 female students, of whom 68 were analysed.}
\cpara{Reports the busy group correctly: 11.15 and 5.83 years (the paper's Table 1). The ratio is 1.9, and the paper reports the difference as significant.}
\cpara{Reports the non-busy group correctly: 7.03 and 6.03 years. The paper says these terms were ``only marginally affected'' by the false statements, and the post does not claim more.}
\cpara{Draws a modest practical lesson. It follows from the crime-report study whichever theory explains it: statements labeled false changed the judgments of busy readers.}
\cpara{Ends with a joke, flagged as made up.}
